intro: If you have spotted cracks, damp patches, a leak that keeps coming back or a wall that seems to be moving, you are probably looking for someone who can tell you what is actually going on. A defect surveyor investigates that specific problem and recommends what to do about it, rather than carrying out a full house purchase survey. Tell us what you have noticed and where you are, and we will introduce you to a suitable UK surveying practice that can quote you directly.
need_heading: What people searching for a defect surveyor usually need
need_lead: Most people who search for a defect surveyor near me have a particular worry about their property and want it looked at properly before deciding what to do next.
needs: You have noticed a crack that seems to be getting wider and want to know whether it is cosmetic or something more serious.
A leak or damp patch keeps returning after a repair, and you want the cause identified rather than patched over again.
You are worried about movement in a wall, floor or roof and want an expert view on whether it needs structural attention.
You are buying a property and the general survey flagged a specific defect that needs a closer look before you commit.
An insurer has asked for a professional report on damage or a defect before it will consider your claim.
context_heading: Understanding what a defect survey involves
context: A defect survey is a targeted inspection of a particular problem, such as cracking, water ingress or structural movement, and the surveyor will recommend repairs rather than survey the whole property. Because the focus is narrow, it helps to describe the symptom clearly and say how long you have noticed it, as this shapes what the surveyor looks at. Some defects turn out to need input from a structural engineer, and a good surveyor will tell you if that is the case.

Many surveyors are members of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS), and RICS-regulated firms must follow professional standards, hold insurance and offer a complaints process. Chartered surveyors use the letters MRICS or FRICS, and you can check the RICS directory to confirm someone's membership. For damp and timber problems, specialists may belong to the Property Care Association, while asbestos surveying is a separate field where you should look for organisations accredited by UKAS.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Describe the defect in your own words, such as a crack, a leak, damp or movement, and where in the property it is.
Say roughly how long you have noticed the problem and whether it appears to be getting worse.
Mention the type and approximate age of the property if you know it, as older buildings often behave differently.
Explain what you want from the visit, whether that is a diagnosis, a repair recommendation or a report for an insurer.
Say whether you are the owner, buying the property or a tenant, as this affects what the surveyor can advise on.
Give your location so we can introduce you to a surveying practice that covers your area.
questions: What kind of defect report will I receive, and will it set out recommended repairs?
Will you be able to tell me whether the problem needs a structural engineer as well?
Is the report suitable to send to my insurer if they have asked for one?
Are you a member of RICS, and is your firm regulated by RICS?
What access will you need around the property, and should I clear anything beforehand?
Will the report explain the likely cause as well as the visible symptoms?

faqs.q: Is a defect survey the same as a homebuyer survey?
faqs.a: No. A defect survey focuses on one specific problem, such as cracking or damp, rather than assessing the whole property. If you are buying and already have a general survey, a defect survey can follow up on something it flagged.

faqs.q: Will the surveyor carry out the repairs too?
faqs.a: Some surveying practices only inspect and report, while others may be able to recommend contractors or arrange further work. It is worth asking upfront so you know what to expect from the visit.

faqs.q: Can a defect surveyor help with an insurance claim?
faqs.a: Insurers sometimes ask for a professional report on the cause and extent of damage before deciding on a claim. Tell the surveyor this is needed so the report covers what your insurer is likely to want.

faqs.q: What if the problem turns out to be structural?
faqs.a: Defect surveyors investigate movement and cracking and can advise whether a structural engineer's input is needed. If so, they can explain what the next step should be rather than leaving you to guess.
